He said nothing about it, however, until their visitor left for the night. As soon as he was gone, he turned to his daughter.

“Congratulations, Jane. You are going to be a very happy woman.”

Jane came straight to him, kissed him, and thanked him for being so kind.

“You’re a good girl,” he replied, “and I’m delighted to think that you will be so happily married. I have no doubt you’ll get along extremely well. Your personalities are certainly similar. You’re both so accommodating that you’ll never make a decision, so relaxed that every servant will cheat you, and so generous that you’ll always spend more than you earn.”

“I hope we won’t. It would be unforgivable for me to be reckless or careless with money.”

“Spend more than they earn! My dear Mr. Bennet,” his wife cried, “what are you talking about? He has four or five thousand a year, and probably more.” She turned to her daughter. “Oh, my dear, dear Jane, I’m so happy! I’m sure I won’t sleep a moment tonight. I knew how it would turn out. I always said it had to happen in the end. I knew you couldn’t be so beautiful for nothing! I remember thinking, the instant I saw him when he first came to Hertfordshire last year, how likely it was that you would get together. Oh, he is the most handsome young man anyone has ever seen!”

Wickham and Lydia were completely forgotten. Jane was now her favorite child without a rival. At that moment no other daughter mattered to her. Jane’s younger sisters soon began cultivating her goodwill, hoping for pleasures she might be able to provide in the future.

Mary asked for permission to use the library at Netherfield, and Kitty pleaded for several balls there every winter.

From that point Bingley naturally came to Longbourn every day, often before breakfast, and always stayed until after supper—unless some barbarous neighbor, impossible to hate enough, had invited him to dinner and he felt obliged to go.

Elizabeth now had little chance to talk with her sister, since Jane could pay attention to nobody else while he was there. But she proved very useful to both of them during the occasional hours when they had to be apart. Whenever Jane was away, Bingley sought Elizabeth out for the pleasure of talking about her. Once Bingley had gone, Jane invariably came to Elizabeth for the same consolation.

“He has made me so happy,” she said one evening. “He told me he had absolutely no idea I was in London last spring!”

The mental abilities we call analytical are themselves difficult to analyze. We recognize them only through what they achieve. We know, among other things, that people who possess these abilities to an exceptional degree take intense pleasure in using them. A strong man enjoys his physical power and welcomes exercise that works his muscles. In the same way, an analyst delights in the mental work of untangling problems. Even the smallest task can please him if it gives his talent something to do. He enjoys mysteries, riddles, and hieroglyphics, solving them with an insight that seems almost supernatural to an ordinary observer. His conclusions appear intuitive, though they are actually produced by the strictest possible method.

The ability to solve problems may well be strengthened by studying mathematics, especially its highest branch. That branch has been called analysis, as though it alone deserved the name, simply and unfairly because it works backward. But calculation is not the same thing as analysis. A chess player, for instance, can calculate without making any effort to analyze. People therefore misunderstand what chess does for the mind. I am not writing a formal study here, only introducing a rather unusual story with a few loosely connected remarks. So I will take this opportunity to say that the simple game of checkers exercises the higher powers of thought more effectively and usefully than all the elaborate trifles of chess. Chess pieces move in different, peculiar ways, and their values differ and change. This leads people to confuse complexity with depth—a common mistake. The game demands intense attention. A moment’s distraction can produce an oversight that damages a player’s position or costs the game. The many possible moves and their complicated connections multiply the opportunities for such mistakes. In nine games out of ten, victory goes to the player who concentrates better, rather than the one with sharper insight. Checkers, by contrast, uses a single kind of move with little variation, reducing the likelihood of careless mistakes. Since attention alone has comparatively little work to do, either player’s advantage must come from greater insight. To make this more concrete, imagine a game of checkers with only four kings left on the board. In such a position, we would naturally expect neither player to overlook anything. If their abilities are at all evenly matched, it is clear that victory can come only from some subtle, carefully devised move that requires a powerful effort of thought.

“Put down your weapons, fellow men, my brothers! If you repent, you will find forgiveness, help, and brotherly love. We care for you because you share our fragile human form. Each of you will find a friend and a host among our soldiers. Must we make enemies of one another when the plague, our common enemy, already hangs over us, rejoicing in a slaughter more cruel than its own?”

Both armies paused. Our soldiers kept a firm grip on their weapons and stared sternly at the enemy. The other men had not laid down their arms, more out of fear than any desire to fight. They looked at one another, each hoping someone would set an example, but they had no leader. Adrian leaped from his horse and went to a man who had just been killed. “He was a man,” he cried, “and now he is dead. Quickly, bind the wounds of those who have fallen! Let no one die. Let no more souls escape through your merciless cuts to tell God how brothers have murdered brothers. Dress their wounds and return them to their friends. Drive the tigers’ hearts from your breasts. Throw away these tools of cruelty and hatred. While our deadly fate gives us this moment’s pause, let every man become a brother, a protector, and a support to the others. Put down your bloodstained weapons, and let some of you hurry to tend these wounds.”

As he spoke, he knelt and lifted a man into his arms. Warm blood poured from the wounded man’s side, and he gasped. Both armies had grown so quiet that everyone could hear his moans. Hearts that moments before had wanted nothing but slaughter now beat anxiously with hope and fear for this one man. Adrian pulled off his military scarf and wrapped it around the sufferer, but he was too late. The man gave a deep sigh. His head dropped back, and his limbs went limp. “He is dead,” Adrian said as the body fell from his arms to the earth. He bowed his head in grief and awe. The whole world’s fate seemed tied to this single death. On both sides, the soldiers threw down their weapons. Even the veterans cried. Our men reached out to their enemies, and love and deep friendship flooded every heart. The two armies mingled, unarmed and hand in hand, discussing only how they could help each other. Their former enemies now stood together. One side regretted its earlier cruelty, the other its recent violence. Together they obeyed the General’s order to head toward London.
